{{IPA|yo|ɔ̄lád͡ʒùwɔ̃̀|lang|Hakeem_Abdul_Olajuwon.wav|link=yes|small=no}}.}} (born January 21, 1963), nicknamed "'''the Dream'''", is a Nigerian and American former professional [[basketball]] player who played 18 seasons in the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA).{{cite magazine|last=Jones|first=Jonathan|date=February 1, 2017|title=Hakeem refuses to be shaken by Trump's Muslim ban|magazine=Sports Illustrated|url=https://www.si.com/nba/2017/02/01/hakeem-olajuwon-donald-trump-muslim-immigration-ban|access-date=July 10, 2021|archive-date=July 13, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210713110253/https://www.si.com/nba/2017/02/01/hakeem-olajuwon-donald-trump-muslim-immigration-ban|url-status=live}} A [[Center (basketball)|center]], he spent a majority of his career with the [[Houston Rockets]] and led them to back-to-back [[NBA championships]] in 1994 and 1995, before a short stint at the end of his career with the [[Toronto Raptors]]. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest players and centers of all time.{{cite web|last=Reimold|first=John|date=April 13, 2011|title=Hakeem Olajuwon Remembered: The Best Center of All Time|url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/663761-remembering-hakeem-olajuwon-the-best-center-of-all-time|access-date=August 7, 2021|website=Bleacher Report|archive-date=August 7, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210807145132/https://bleacherreport.com/articles/663761-remembering-hakeem-olajuwon-the-best-center-of-all-time|url-status=live}}{{cite web|last=Reardon|first=Logan|date=June 8, 2021|title=Where does Bill Russell rank among best centers in NBA history?|website=NBC Sports|url=https://www.nbcsports.com/boston/celtics/where-does-bill-russell-rank-among-best-centers-nba-history|access-date=July 10, 2021|archive-date=April 5, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220405054451/https://www.nbcsports.com/boston/celtics/where-does-bill-russell-rank-among-best-centers-nba-history|url-status=live}}{{cite web|date=March 6, 2007|title=The game's greatest giants ever|website=ESPN.com|url=http://www.espn.com/nba/dailydime?page=dailydime-GreatestCenters|access-date=July 10, 2021|archive-date=April 15, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220415181050/http://www.espn.com/nba/dailydime?page=dailydime-GreatestCenters|url-status=live}} Born in [[Lagos]], Nigeria, Olajuwon traveled from his home country to play for the [[University of Houston]] under head coach [[Guy Lewis]]. His college career for the [[Houston Cougars men's basketball|Cougars]] included three trips to the [[Final Four]]. Olajuwon was drafted by the Houston Rockets with the first overall selection of the [[1984 NBA draft]], a draft well known for its immense talent, which also included players such as [[Michael Jordan]], [[Charles Barkley]], and [[John Stockton]]. He combined with the {{convert|7|ft|4|in|cm|adj=on}} [[Ralph Sampson]] to form a duo dubbed the "Twin Towers". The two led the Rockets to the [[1986 NBA Finals]], where they lost in six games to the [[Boston Celtics]]. After Sampson was traded to the [[Golden State Warriors]] in 1988, Olajuwon became the Rockets' undisputed leader. He led the league in [[Rebound (basketball)|rebounding]] twice (1989, 1990) and [[Block (basketball)|blocks]] three times (1990, 1991, 1993). Despite very nearly being traded during a bitter contract dispute before the 1992–93 season, he remained in Houston. He became the first non-American to be an [[NBA All-Star]] and start in an [[NBA All-Star Game]], the first non-American to win the NBA [[National Basketball Association Most Valuable Player Award|MVP]], the first non-American to win NBA [[NBA Defensive Player of the Year|Defensive Player of the Year]], and in the 1993–94 season, he became and remains the only player in NBA history to win the NBA [[National Basketball Association Most Valuable Player Award|MVP]], [[NBA Defensive Player of the Year|Defensive Player of the Year]], and [[NBA Finals MVP|Finals MVP]] awards in the same season. His Rockets won back-to-back championships. [[1994 NBA Finals|The Rockets' 1994 championship]] against the [[New York Knicks]] was the first in franchise history, with Olajuwon avenging his college championship loss to [[Patrick Ewing]]. [[1995 NBA Finals|The following year]], after [[1994–95 Houston Rockets season|a lackluster regular season]], Olajuwon's Rockets swept [[Shaquille O'Neal]]'s [[Orlando Magic]] in 4 games in the NBA Finals. Olajuwon was a member of the [[Basketball at the 1996 Summer Olympics – Men's tournament|1996 Olympic gold medal-winning]] [[United States national basketball team]], and was selected as one of the [[50 Greatest Players in NBA History]]. He was inducted into the [[Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame]] in 2008 and the [[FIBA Hall of Fame]] in 2016. In October 2021, Olajuwon was honored as one of the league's greatest players of all time by being named to the [[NBA 75th Anniversary Team]].{{cite web|url=https://www.nba.com/news/nba-75th-anniversary-team-announced|title=NBA 75th Anniversary Team announced|website=NBA.com|date=October 21, 2021|access-date=March 16, 2022|archive-date=October 25, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211025195243/https://www.nba.com/news/nba-75th-anniversary-team-announced|url-status=live}} He ended his career as the league's all-time leader in [[block (basketball)|blocks]] (3,830), is one of four NBA players to record a [[quadruple-double]], and is the all-time leader in [[Double-double#Five-by-five|5x5]] games (when a player has at least 5 points, 5 rebounds, 5 assists, 5 steals and 5 blocks) with six.{{Cite web |date=November 1, 2024 |title=What is a 5x5 game in basketball? A [[Center (basketball)|center]], he spent most of his career with the [[Utah Jazz]] of the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA). He played [[college basketball]] for the [[Kansas Jayhawks men's basketball|Kansas Jayhawks]].

In 2026, Ostertag was elected as mayor of [[Mount Vernon, Texas]].
